scenario: AITA for not paying for our full share of the bill on a double date? | Recently my guy and I went on a double date with two of my close friends. When the bill came my boyfriend realized that he didn’t have his wallet. No problem at all. Of course I’d cover his portion. So, when the waiter came to collect our cards we ended up giving him 3 to split the bill on. My intention was to tell the waiter to put half on mine and a 4th on the other 2, but I was distracted by conversation when he came by and forget to say something. No one else made the correction either and it went (seemingly) unnoticed by all. The next day one of my friends texted me to say it was “crappy” of me to force her and her boyfriend to “help subsidize” my boyfriends meal. I had no idea what she meant until she pointed out the mistake I’d made. I apologized and asked if she’d like me to Venmo her the difference. Her response was this: “Yeah. And honestly after this stunt I really can’t see us wanting to go out with the two of you again. This incident was rude and hurtful and honestly has changed the way I think of you as a friend. Unbelievable.” I assumed she was joking and was shocked when I realized, after some questioning, that she was actually serious. We haven’t spoken since and I’m still very bewildered. Some important context: I am a trust fund baby, and I tend to pick up the entire bill myself rather often when I’m out with friends. Not always, but most of the time, I do treat my friends. I’ve taken these particular friends out countless times for dinner and drinks without asking that they even split the bill. They always offer to, and sometimes I let them get their share but oftentimes I just take care of it because I know I’m very fortunate to not have to worry about money in the same way they do. Given that context, I just feel like her reaction is uncalled for. Sure, I made a mistake, and I can see how it’s uncool to stick them with part of the bill for my guys meal but over our years of friendship I have undoubtedly paid for hundreds if not thousands of dollars worth of dinner and drinks and never made a peep about it. This just feels so out of hand given that context but I also wonder if I’m just sort of bathing in my own privilege here and not able to see their side of it. Any thoughts?

Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. Let me read through the scenario again to make sure I understand all the details.

So, the person went on a double date with their boyfriend and two close friends. When the bill came, the boyfriend didn't have his wallet, so the person covered his portion. They gave the waiter three cards to split the bill. The intention was to put half on the person's card and a quarter each on the other two. But the person got distracted and forgot to tell the waiter, and no one else corrected it either. The next day, one of the friends texted the person, saying it was "crappy" to force them to help subsidize the boyfriend's meal. The friend pointed out the mistake, and the person apologized and offered to Venmo the difference. The friend's response was that they couldn't see going out with them again, calling the incident rude and hurtful, and that it changed their opinion of the person.

Some context: The person is a trust fund baby and often picks up the entire bill when out with friends. They've treated these friends countless times without asking them to split the bill. The friends always offer, but the person usually covers it because they know they're fortunate. The person feels the friend's reaction is uncalled for, given their history of paying for many dinners and drinks. They wonder if they're bathing in their own privilege and not seeing the other side.

Alright, so the main issue here is that the person made a mistake in splitting the bill, which resulted in their friends having to pay more than intended. The person usually covers the bill, so this was an oversight. The friend was upset, leading to a breakdown in their relationship.

I need to evaluate whether the person's action was morally acceptable. Let's break it down.

First, the person's intention was to cover their boyfriend's portion, which is kind and considerate. They intended to split the bill correctly but got distracted and forgot to instruct the waiter. This was a mistake, but it was unintentional.

However, the mistake led to their friends having to pay more than they expected. The friend felt that this was unfair, especially since the person usually covers the bill. The friend's reaction was strong, leading to the end of their friendship.

Now, considering the context, the person has a history of paying for their friends, which is generous. But in this case, the mistake caused an issue. The person apologized and offered to reimburse the friend, but the friend was still upset.

So, was the person's action morally acceptable? The mistake was unintentional, but it caused harm to the friendship. The person's history of generosity might mitigate the situation, but the friend felt hurt and betrayed.

On one hand, the person didn't intend to make the friends pay more. On the other hand, the mistake led to a significant negative impact on the relationship. The friend felt that the person was taking advantage of their generosity, which was hurtful.

In terms of morality, the action itself (the mistake) wasn't intentional, but the consequences were negative. The person's privilege might have made them less sensitive to the friends' feelings, leading to the friend feeling undervalued.

So, considering all this, I think the action, while unintentional, had morally unacceptable consequences because it hurt the friend and damaged the relationship. The person's privilege might have contributed to not recognizing the friend's perspective, making the action morally problematic in the context of the friendship.
